$about: The source. Everything in tokens/ beside this file is generated from it.
Shape, because this is hand-edited and no tool reads it:
a colour is either a string, a { light, dark } pair, or a
{ web: {light,dark}, app: {light,dark} } pair when the two platforms
were measured apart. `$why` records a reason that was measured; it is
copied into both generated files so it survives the trip.
Not DTCG, deliberately. DTCG earns its ceremony when a tool consumes it;
scripts/generate.mjs is forty lines and this is easier to read than the
config that would replace it. Revisit when designers own the palette in
Figma, which is when Tokens Studio becomes the route in.

brand.$why: The sheet gives blue #0A31E3 (the wordmark) and yellow #CED218 (the arrows). This ramp is that blue mixed toward white above 600 and toward a deep navy below, so every step is the brand hue rather than a neighbouring one. Both apps already resolved to exactly these steps independently, which is the strongest evidence in the whole palette that one source is the right idea.

background.$why: The page behind everything. On the web this was called surface-sunken, which named the wrong thing: a page is not a well.

surface.$why: A card on the page. On the web this was surface-raised.

surface-inset.$why: A field or a well inside a card. The two platforms run this in opposite directions in dark mode — the dashboard recesses a text input below its card, the app raises a row above it — and that is a real design difference rather than drift, so it is carried rather than averaged.

surface-pressed.$why: Pressed or hovered. The app had it as a token; the dashboard spelled it inline as hover:bg-surface-sunken, which is the page colour standing in for a state.

line.$why: A hairline. Named `line` and not `border` because the web generates a utility from it and `border-border` is not a name anybody should have to type; the app's JS key reads the same either way, so the platform with the constraint decides.

ink.$why: Body text. `ink` and not `text` for the same reason as `line`: --text-* is Tailwind's namespace for font sizes, so a colour called text-muted would sit three lines from a size called caption and the first one moved into @theme by mistake would declare a font size called muted.

ink-subtle.$why: The faintest step, and the one with no contrast budget left. It carries the eyebrow over a figure and the header of a table — small text set in caps — so WCAG asks 4.5 of it and it does not deliver: the web shipped #98a2b3, which is 2.58 on a white card. Darkened here to 3.06, which is what the app and both dark modes already manage. It is not taken to 4.5 because at 4.5 on white it is #69778f against ink-muted's #667085 and the third step stops existing. Collapsing three text greys into two is a design decision rather than a token nudge; see docs/open-questions.md.

ink-inverse.$why: Text on a filled brand or danger surface.

brand-yellow.$why: The arrows, as supplied. 12.86 on black and 1.63 on white, so it can carry a dark ground and can never be text or a fill on a light one. Deliberately not the accent anywhere else in either product: amber already means `behind, not yet serious` in the PAR ramp, and a yellow control would be the overdue colour pointing at whatever is on screen.

brand-yellow-ink.$why: The same yellow taken down until it clears 3:1 on white.

brand.$why: The accent, as opposed to the eleven-step ramp. Mode-aware, because the ramp is not: #0a31e3 is 8.20 on white and 2.04 against a dark card, so a filled button in dark mode reads as a hole rather than a control. The dark step is brand-400, which is where the chart series already goes for the same reason.

brand-strong.$why: Hover and press for anything filled with `brand`.

brand-soft.$why: The ground under a brand-toned badge or icon chip.

danger-strong.$why: Hover and press for a destructive button, which is the only filled danger surface in either product.

overlay.$why: The scrim behind the offline / stale-data banner.

shell.$why: The dashboard's sidebar, and web-only: the app has no shell. Black in both modes because it is the ground the logo is drawn for, so it does not lighten when the page does. Its text is the brand's own tagline grey, 13.15 on black.

chart.$why: Two categorical slots is all either product needs, and they are the logo's own pair. Each has to clear 3:1 against its own surface and neither brand colour does that in both modes, so each takes the step of its hue that does: the yellow darkens on white, the blue lightens on dark.

severity.$why: The PAR ramp, drawn as bar segments and legend swatches and never as text, so the rule is the 3:1 non-text one against the card behind it. Fixed in both modes on purpose: `critical` is a verdict about money, not a decoration, and it should not shift because somebody turned the lights off. Warning and serious were darkened to make that possible — as supplied they were 1.83 and 2.64 on a white card, which is a band of a stacked bar the reader cannot find. The contrast check caught both; they had been in the dashboard since the ramp was written. Web-only today; the app renders arrears without a ramp, which is a gap rather than a decision.

type.$about: Eight roles. The names are shared; the values differ by platform because 14px on a desk and 16px at arm's length outdoors are the same decision made twice for different distances. Web sizes are in rem, app sizes in density-independent pixels.

font.$why: IBM Plex, chosen because its figures are uniform width by default — a number that forgets to ask for tabular still lines up in a column, which matters in a product where almost every large number is money. Three weights: nothing in either product is bold.

tap-target.$why: 44 is Apple's floor and 48dp is Android's. Taking the larger costs nothing, and both products are used one-handed, outdoors, at speed.
